title: An article in the Bande Mataram daily (1906)
body: In 1906, Bipin Chandra Pal launched the English daily Bande Mataram, and Aurobindo Ghose soon took charge of it. An article of 4 September 1906 said, in part: 'We objected so strongly to this measure [Bengal's Partition, because] it was professedly wanted by the Government to create a Mahomedan province with Dacca as its capital, and the evident object of it was to sow discord between the Hindus and the Mahomedans in a Province that had never known it in the whole history of the present British connection. ... This agitation is not an agitation merely against Partition ... The attainment of absolute national autonomy - it is this alone that will settle down this movement.' The paper also added National Education to Swadeshi and boycott and spelt out a 'doctrine of passive resistance' to the colonial power.

title: The Lahore resolution of 1929
body: In December 1929, the Lahore session of the Congress passed a resolution demanding Purna Swaraj. An extract reads: 'We believe that it is the inalienable right of the Indian people, as of any other people, to have freedom and to enjoy the fruits of their toil and have the necessities of life, so that they may have full opportunities of growth. We believe also that if any government deprives a people of these rights and oppresses them the people have a further right to alter it or to abolish it. The British government in India has not only deprived the Indian people of their freedom but has based itself on the exploitation of the masses, and has ruined India economically, politically, culturally, and spiritually. We believe, therefore, that India must sever the British connection and attain Purna Swaraj or complete independence.' A year earlier, the Motilal Nehru Report had asked only for Dominion status.

title: Quit India, August 1942
body: In August 1942, after rejecting the Cripps Mission's offer, Mahatma Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement with the call 'Do or Die'. The demand was that the British must leave India at once. Virtually the entire Congress leadership was arrested, yet mass protests and rallies erupted across the country. Workers went on strike, students left schools, and telegraph poles were uprooted. Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan kept the underground movement going. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the national flag at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay and then went underground for nearly four years, editing secret bulletins. In Assam, 17-year-old Kanaklata Barua was shot dead while leading a procession to hoist the flag at the Gohpur police station. Viceroy Linlithgow called the movement 'by far the most serious rebellion since 1857'. It was brutally suppressed, with over 100,000 people imprisoned.
